newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Timor's Horta pessimistic about U.N. talks in June.
newsitem.headline: Timor's Horta pessimistic about U.N. talks in June.

text.p: East Timorese independence leader Jose Ramos Horta, co-winner of the 1996 Nobel peace prize, said on Friday that new U.N.-led talks on Timor would take place in June but their success was in doubt.
He said he had the utmost confidence in U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and his special envoy, Jamsheed Marker, a former Pakistani U.N. ambassador.
But he said Indonesia showed no sign of softening its harsh rule despite promises to the contrary.
"The situation on the ground leaves no room for optimism," he said. "There is no sign whatsover that Indonesia might consider to negotiate in good faith."

However, he said now that Indonesia's ruling party had triumphed in the just-concluded elections -- which he called a "complete fraud" -- perhaps President Suharto "would feel motivated to address the issue of East Timor."

U.N. officials said the talks, led by Annan, most likely would be in New York among the Indonesian and Portuguese foreign ministers but that tentative dates of June 19-20 could slip to the end of June.

Horta met privately with U.S. Ambassador Bill Richardson as well as other U.N. envoys, including South Korean ambassador Park Soo Gil. He said he was honoured at his meeting with Richardson, the highest level U.S. official he has met and was assured of "his strong interest on this."
Horta, whose movement for years had been isolated abroad, saw Annan earlier this year, the first time in 22 years that a U.N. chief had agreed to meet an East Timorese representative.

Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 after Portugal withdrew from its former colony, which Indonesia annexed the following year as its 27th province. Guerrillas of the Fretilin independence movement continued for years to mount attacks on Indonesian troops.
The international community does not recognise the annexation, and talks have dragged on since 1983.
Horta, a long-time campaigner for self-determination, said Timorese would bend over backwards to stop guerrilla activities and demonstrations if there were any sign of compromise by Indonesia.
But Indonesia, he said, had to come up with concrete measures: reduce its more than 20,000 troops in East Timor, release prisoners and stop torturing those in its prisons.
"Human rights have deteriorated, there are hundreds of arrests, torture is rampant and there is increased militarization of the territory," he said.
"And this must be independently verified. We are not going to accept their word because they have "lied for many years."
East Timorese, he said, were not the only victims of the government and army's harsh rule, adding: "When it comes to repression no one can accuse the regime of discriminatory policies."
